q-34510.name: Question 1
q-34510.problem:
The matrix $A$ is given below. Let ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$, and ${a}_{3}$ are the respective columns of $A.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{a}_{1},{a}_{3}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(A).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${a}_{2}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}.$ 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 4 \\ -2 & -6 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$
q-34510.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $A$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 4 \\ -2 & -6 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 13\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{13}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-4){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $3$rd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(A)$ is $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{3}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $2$nd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${a}_{2}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}={{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{{(0)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{3}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{3}=3\cdot 0=0.$

A=[134−2−65]

EXPLANATION

First, we reduce the matrix A to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

A=[134−2−65]R2:=R2+2R1∼[1340013]R2:=113R2∼[134001]R1:=R1+(−4)R2∼[130001]

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the 1st and 3rd columns. So, a basis of Col(A) is {a1,a3}, that is to say,

B={[1−2],[45]}.

Now, since the 2nd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express a2 as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

[3−6]⏟a2=(3)⏟x1⋅[1−2]⏟a1+(0)⏟x3⋅[45]⏟a3.

This gives us x1⋅x3=3⋅0=0.

q-75946.name: Question 2
q-75946.problem:
The matrix $P$ is given below. Let ${p}_{1}$, ${p}_{2}$, and ${p}_{3}$ be the respective columns of $P.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(P).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${p}_{3}={x}_{1}{p}_{1}+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}.$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$
q-75946.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $P$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(P)$ is $\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${p}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{p}_{3}}={{(-2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{p}_{1}}+{{(1)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{p}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=(-2)\cdot 1=-2.$

q-75951.name: Question 3
q-75951.problem:
The matrix $Q$ is given below. Let ${q}_{1}$, ${q}_{2}$, and ${q}_{3}$ be the respective columns of $Q.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(Q).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${q}_{3}={x}_{1}{q}_{1}+{x}_{2}{q}_{2}.$

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$
q-75951.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $Q$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$ is $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${q}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{3}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{1}}+{{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 2=4.$

q-111515.name: Question 4
q-111515.problem:
The matrix $V$ is given below. Let ${v}_{1}$, ${v}_{2}$,  ${v}_{3}$, and ${v}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $V.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(V).$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${v}_{4}={x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}.$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -3 & -3 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}]
$$
q-111515.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $V$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -2 & -3 & -3 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & -6 \\ -2 & 6 & 8 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 & 18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 & 18\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(V)$ is $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $4$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${v}_{4}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3 \\ 12\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{4}}={{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+{{(3)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=3\cdot 3=9.$

q-111807.name: Question 5
q-111807.problem:
The matrix $R$ is given below. Let ${r}_{1}$, ${r}_{2}$,  ${r}_{3}$ and ${r}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $R.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{r}_{1},{r}_{2},{r}_{3}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(R).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${r}_{4}={x}_{1}{r}_{1}+{x}_{2}{r}_{2}+{x}_{3}{r}_{3}.$ 

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -3 & -2 \\ 3 & 5 & -7 & -8 \\ 4 & 6 & -10 & -10\end{aligned}]
$$
q-111807.worked_solution:
First, we reduce the matrix $R$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}R & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -3 & -2 \\ 3 & 5 & -7 & -8 \\ 4 & 6 & -10 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & -2 \\ 4 & 6 & -10 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(R)$ is $\{{r}_{1},{r}_{2}\}.$ 

Therefore, we conclude that $B=\{{r}_{1},{r}_{2},{r}_{3}\}$ is not a basis of $\text{Col}(R).$
